{{Short description|Several sets of circles associated with Apollonius of Perga}}
The '''circles of Apollonius''' are any of several sets of circles associated with [[Apollonius of Perga]], a renowned [[ancient Greece|Greek]] [[geometer]].  Most of these circles are found in  [[plane (geometry)|planar]] [[Euclidean geometry]], but analogs have been defined on other surfaces; for example, counterparts on the surface of a sphere can be defined through [[stereographic projection]].

The main uses of this term are fivefold:
# Apollonius showed that a circle can be defined as the set of points in a plane that have a specified ''ratio'' of distances to two fixed points, known as [[focus (geometry)|foci]].  This '''[[Apollonian circles|Apollonian circle]]''' is the basis of the Apollonius pursuit problem.  It is a particular case of the first family described in #2.
# The '''[[Apollonian circles]]''' are two families of mutually [[orthogonal]] circles.  The first family consists of the circles with all possible distance ratios to two fixed foci (the same circles as in #1), whereas the second family consists of all possible circles that pass through both foci.  These circles form the basis of [[bipolar coordinates]].
# The '''circles of Apollonius of a triangle''' are three circles, each of which passes through one vertex of the triangle and maintains a constant ratio of distances to the other two.  The [[isodynamic point]]s and [[Lemoine line]] of a triangle can be solved using these circles of Apollonius.
# '''[[Problem of Apollonius|Apollonius's problem]]''' is to construct circles that are simultaneously tangent to three specified circles.  The solutions to this problem are sometimes called the '''circles of Apollonius'''.
# The '''[[Apollonian gasket]]'''—one of the first [[fractal]]s ever described—is a set of mutually tangent circles, formed by solving Apollonius's problem iteratively.

==Apollonius's definition of a circle==
{{Main|Circle#Circle of Apollonius}}

{{anchor|fig-def}}
[[File:Apollonius circle definition labels.svg|thumb|right|Apollonius's definition of a circle]]

A circle is usually defined as the set of points {{mvar|P}} at a given distance {{mvar|r}} (the circle's radius) from a given point (the circle's center).  However, there are other, equivalent definitions of a circle.  Apollonius discovered that a circle could be defined as the set of points {{mvar|P}} that have a given ''ratio'' of distances {{math|1=''k'' = {{sfrac|''d''<sub>1</sub>|''d''<sub>2</sub>}}}} to two given points (labeled {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} in the figure).  These two points are sometimes called the [[focus (geometry)|foci]].

===Proof using vectors in Euclidean spaces===
Let {{math|''d''{{sub|1}}}}, {{math|''d''{{sub|2}}}} be non-equal positive real numbers.
Let {{mvar|C}} be the internal division point of {{mvar|AB}} in the ratio {{math|''d''{{sub|1}} : ''d''{{sub|2}}}} and {{mvar|D}} the external division point of {{mvar|AB}} in the same ratio, {{math|''d''{{sub|1}} : ''d''{{sub|2}}}}.

<math display=block>
  \overrightarrow{PC} = \frac{d_2\overrightarrow{PA} + d_1\overrightarrow{PB}}{d_2 + d_1},\quad 
  \overrightarrow{PD} = \frac{d_2\overrightarrow{PA} - d_1\overrightarrow{PB}}{d_2 - d_1}.
</math>

Then,
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  &PA : PB = d_1 : d_2. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& d_2|\overrightarrow{PA}| = d_1|\overrightarrow{PB}|. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& d_2^2|\overrightarrow{PA}|^2 = d_1^2|\overrightarrow{PB}|^2. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& (d_2\overrightarrow{PA} + d_1\overrightarrow{PB})\cdot (d_2\overrightarrow{PA} - d_1\overrightarrow{PB}) = 0. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& \frac{d_2\overrightarrow{PA} + d_1\overrightarrow{PB}}{d_2 + d_1}\cdot \frac{d_2\overrightarrow{PA} - d_1\overrightarrow{PB}}{d_2 - d_1} = 0. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& \overrightarrow{PC} \cdot \overrightarrow{PD} = 0. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& \overrightarrow{PC} = \vec{0} \vee \overrightarrow{PD} = \vec{0} \vee \overrightarrow{PC} \perp \overrightarrow{PD}. \\
  \Leftrightarrow{}& P = C \vee P = D \vee \angle CPD = 90^\circ.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, the point {{mvar|P}} is on the circle which has the diameter {{mvar|CD}}.
{{clear}}

===Proof using the angle bisector theorem===
[[File:Proof of Apollonius' definition of a circle.svg|thumb|right|Proof of Apollonius's definition of a circle]]

First consider the point {{mvar|C}} on the line segment between {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, satisfying the ratio. By the definition
<math display="block">\frac{|AP|}{|BP|}=\frac{|AC|}{|BC|}</math>
and from the converse of the [[angle bisector theorem]], the angles {{math|1=''&alpha;'' = &angle;&hairsp;''APC''}} and {{math|1=''&beta;'' = &angle;''CPB''}} are equal.

Next take the other point {{mvar|D}} on the extended line {{mvar|AB}} that satisfies the ratio. So
<math display="block">\frac{|AP|}{|BP|}=\frac{|AD|}{|BD|}.</math>
Also take some other point {{mvar|Q}} anywhere on the extended line {{mvar|AP}}. Again by the converse of the angle bisector theorem, the line {{mvar|PD}} bisects the exterior angle {{math|&angle;''QPB''}}. Hence, {{math|1=''&gamma;'' = &angle;&hairsp;''BPD''}} and {{math|1=''&delta;'' = &angle;&hairsp;''QPD''}} are equal and {{math|1=''&beta;'' + ''&gamma;'' = 90&deg;}}. Hence by [[Thales's theorem]] {{mvar|P}} lies on the circle which has {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}} as a diameter.

===Apollonius pursuit problem===

The Apollonius pursuit problem is one of finding whether a ship leaving from one point {{mvar|A}} at speed {{math|''v''<sub>A</sub>}} will intercept another ship leaving a different point {{mvar|B}} at speed {{math|''v''<sub>B</sub>}}.  The minimum time in interception of the two ships is calculated by means of straight-line paths. If the ships' speeds are held constant, their speed ratio is defined by {{mvar|μ}}. If both ships collide or meet at a future point, {{mvar|I}}, then the distances of each are related by the equation:<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1049/iet-cta.2019.0541 |title=Optimal guidance strategy for the defense of a non-manoeuvrable target in 3-dimensions |year=2020 |last1=Weintraub |first1=Isaac |last2=Garcia |first2=Eloy |last3=Pachter |first3=Meir |journal=IET Control Theory & Applications |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=1531–1538 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

<math display=block>a = \mu b</math>

With the [[Euclidean distance|distances]] in question being:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  a &= \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \\
  b &= \sqrt{(d-x)^2 + y^2} 
\end{align}</math>

Substituting in {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}} and squaring both sides, we obtain:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  a^2 &= \mu^2 b^2 \\
  x^2 + y^2 &= \mu^2 \left[(d-x)^2 + y^2 \right] \\
            &= \mu^2 \left[d^2 + x^2 - 2dx + y^2 \right] \\
            &= x^2 \mu^2 + y^2\mu^2 + d^2\mu^2 - 2dx \mu^2
\end{align}</math>

Bringing to the left-hand side:
<math display=block>x^2 - x^2\mu^2 + y^2 - y^2\mu^2 - d^2\mu^2 + 2dx\mu^2 = 0</math>

Factoring:
<math display=block>x^2(1-\mu^2) + y^2(1-\mu^2) - d^2\mu^2 + 2dx\mu^2 = 0</math>

Dividing by <math>1-\mu^2</math> :
<math display=block>x^2 + y^2 - \frac{d^2\mu^2}{1-\mu^2} + \frac{2dx\mu^2}{1-\mu^2} = 0</math>

Completing the square:
<math display=block>\left(x+ \frac{d\mu^2}{1-\mu^2}\right)^2- \frac{d^2\mu^4}{(1-\mu^2)^2} - \frac{d^2 \mu^2}{1-\mu^2} + y^2 = 0</math>

Bring non-squared terms to the right-hand side:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\left( x + \frac{d\mu^2}{1-\mu^2} \right)^2 + y^2
  &= \frac{d^2\mu^4}{(1-\mu^2)^2} + \frac{d^2 \mu^2}{1-\mu^2}\\[2pt]
  &= \frac{d^2 \mu^4}{(1-\mu^2)^2} + \frac{d^2 \mu^2}{1-\mu^2} \frac{(1-\mu^2)}{(1-\mu^2)}\\[2pt]
  &= \frac{d^2\mu^4+d^2\mu^2-d^2\mu^4}{(1-\mu^2)^2}\\[2pt]
  &= \frac{d^2 \mu^2}{(1-\mu^2)^2}
\end{align}</math>

Then:
<math display=block>\left( x + \frac{d\mu^2}{1-\mu^2}\right)^2 + y^2 = \left( \frac{d \mu}{1-\mu^2} \right)^2</math>

Therefore, the point must lie on a circle as defined by Apollonius, with their starting points as the foci.

==Circles sharing a radical axis==
{{main|Apollonian circles}}

[[File:Apollonian circles.svg|thumb|right|A set of Apollonian circles. Every blue circle intersects every red circle at a right angle, and vice versa. Every red circle passes through the two foci, which correspond to points {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} in the [[#fig-def|figure above]].]]

The circles defined by the Apollonian pursuit problem for the same two points {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, but with varying ratios of the two speeds, are disjoint from each other and form a continuous family that cover the entire plane; this family of circles is known as a ''hyperbolic pencil''. Another family of circles, the circles that pass through both {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, are also called a pencil, or more specifically an ''elliptic pencil''. These two pencils of [[Apollonian circles]] intersect each other at [[right angle]]s and form the basis of the [[bipolar coordinates|bipolar coordinate system]]. Within each pencil, any two circles have the same [[radical axis]]; the two radical axes of the two pencils are perpendicular, and the centers of the circles from one pencil lie on the radical axis of the other pencil.

{{clear}}

==Solutions to Apollonius's problem==
{{main|Problem of Apollonius}}

[[File:Apollonius8ColorMultiplyV2.svg|right|thumb|[[Apollonius's problem]] may have up to eight solutions.  The three given circles are shown in black, whereas the solution circles are colored.]]

In [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean plane geometry]], '''Apollonius's problem''' is to construct [[circle]]s that are [[tangent]] to three given circles in a plane.

Three given circles generically have eight different circles that are tangent to them, in four conjugate pairs. Each pair corresponds to one of the four ways of partitioning the three given circles into two subsets, separated from each other by the tangent circle.

{{clear}}

==Apollonian gasket==
{{main|Apollonian gasket}}

[[File:Apollonian gasket.svg|thumb|right|A symmetrical Apollonian gasket, also called the Leibniz packing, after its inventor [[Gottfried Leibniz]]]]

By solving Apollonius's problem repeatedly to find the inscribed circle, the [[wikt:interstice|interstice]]s between mutually tangential circles can be filled arbitrarily finely, forming an [[Apollonian gasket]], also known as a ''Leibniz packing'' or an ''Apollonian packing''.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Kasner, E. |author2=Supnick, F. |year=1943 |title=The Apollonian packing of circles |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA |volume=29 |issue=11 |pages=378&ndash;384 |doi=10.1073/pnas.29.11.378 |pmc=1078636 |pmid=16588629 |bibcode=1943PNAS...29..378K |doi-access=free}}</ref>  This gasket is a [[fractal]], being self-similar and having a [[Hausdorff dimension|dimension]] ''d'' that is not known exactly but is roughly 1.3,<ref name="boyd_1973">{{cite journal |last1=Boyd|first1=David W.|year=1973 |title=Improved Bounds for the Disk Packing Constants |journal=[[Aequationes Mathematicae]] |volume=9 |pages=99&ndash;106 |doi=10.1007/BF01838194 |doi-access= |s2cid=121089590}}<br />{{cite journal |last1=Boyd|first1=David W.|year=1973 |title=The Residual Set Dimension of the Apollonian Packing |journal=[[Mathematika]] |volume=20 |pages=170&ndash;174 |doi=10.1112/S0025579300004745 |issue=2}}<br />{{cite journal |last=McMullen |first=Curtis, T. |title=Hausdorff dimension and conformal dynamics III: Computation of dimension |url=https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/papers/home/text/papers/dimIII/dimIII.pdf |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=120 |year=1998 |pages=691&ndash;721 |doi=10.1353/ajm.1998.0031 |issue=4 |s2cid=15928775}}</ref> which is higher than that of a [[regular curve|regular]] (or [[rectifiable curve|rectifiable]]) curve (''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1) but less than that of a plane (''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2).  The Apollonian gasket was first described by [[Gottfried Leibniz]] in the 17th century, and is a curved precursor of the 20th-century [[Sierpiński triangle]].<ref>{{cite book |author=[[Benoit Mandelbrot |Mandelbrot, B.]] |year=1983 |title=The Fractal Geometry of Nature |publisher=W.H. Freeman |location=New York |isbn=978-0-7167-1186-5 |page=[https://archive.org/details/fractalgeometryo00beno/page/170 170] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/fractalgeometryo00beno/page/170}}<br />{{cite book |author=Aste, T., and [[Denis Weaire |Weaire, D.]] |year=2008 |title=The Pursuit of Perfect Packing |title-link=The Pursuit of Perfect Packing |edition=2nd |publisher=Taylor and Francis |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4200-6817-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/pursuitperfectpa00weai_920/page/n134 131]&ndash;138}}</ref>  The Apollonian gasket also has deep connections to other fields of mathematics; for example, it is the limit set of [[Kleinian group]]s;<ref>{{cite book |author=[[David Mumford |Mumford, D.]], Series, C., and Wright, D. |year=2002 |title=Indra's Pearls: The Vision of Felix Klein |url=https://archive.org/details/indraspearlsvisi00mumf |url-access=limited |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-35253-3 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/indraspearlsvisi00mumf/page/n213 196]&ndash;223}}</ref> see also [[Circle packing theorem]].

{{clear}}
==Isodynamic points of a triangle==
The '''circles of Apollonius''' may also denote three special circles <math>\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\mathcal{C}_{3}</math> defined by an arbitrary triangle <math>\mathrm{A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}}</math>.  The circle <math>\mathcal{C}_{1}</math> is defined as the unique circle passing through the triangle vertex <math>\mathrm{A_{1}}</math> that maintains a constant ratio of distances to the other two vertices <math>\mathrm{A_{2}}</math> and <math>\mathrm{A_{3}}</math> (cf. Apollonius's definition of the [[circle]] above).  Similarly, the circle <math>\mathcal{C}_{2}</math> is defined as the unique circle passing through the triangle vertex <math>\mathrm{A_{2}}</math> that maintains a constant ratio of distances to the other two vertices <math>\mathrm{A_{1}}</math> and <math>\mathrm{A_{3}}</math>, and so on for the circle <math>\mathcal{C}_{3}</math>.

All three circles intersect the [[circumcircle]] of the [[triangle]] [[orthogonal]]ly.  All three circles pass through two points, which are known as the [[isodynamic point]]s <math>S</math> and <math>S^{\prime}</math> of the triangle.  The line connecting these common intersection points is the [[radical axis]] for all three circles.  The two isodynamic points are [[circle inversion|inverses]] of each other relative to the [[circumcircle]] of the triangle.

The centers of these three circles fall on a single line (the '''[[Lemoine line]]''').  This line is perpendicular to the radical axis, which is the line determined by the isodynamic points.
